Jon Jang
Part II

Jon Jang continues to be in the forefront of world music composition. His first symphony, “The Chinese-American Symphony,” premiered in 2007 in Sacramento, CA. His musical collaborations have included recordings with the pipa virtuoso Min Xiao-Fen and the late percussionist Max Roach.
This interview took place in Clinton, NY on October 9, 2013 and was conducted by Monk Rowe, director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
I’m happy to do interview part II with Jon Jang here at Hamilton College, and it’s been ten years since you were here before. What have you been doing all that time?

Well the first thing I want to mention is that I became the first Chinese-American, the first American born Chinese to compose a symphony which was called “The Chinese- American Symphony” that honored the Chinese railroad workers who built the first transcontinental railroad in the United States. So I’m very proud of that achievement, but I also want to recognize that that’s an important part of my legacy, my personal legacy, but as well as in America, or I would say, an advancement of American transformation.

How does something like that come about? You have this, your own passion for history, American history and the role of Chinese people in it, and you want to compose music that addresses it, but what’s the process of getting a symphony written and than having people play it?

Oh it’s been a lifelong process. And that’s actually somewhat of a separate question, but then what I would describe that this has been an idea that germinated since my childhood. During the 1960’s I spent my childhood in Palo Alto, and that’s located, that’s where Stanford University is located. And I was often reminded that Stanford built the railroad. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-

So in 1963 the Chinese Historical Society of America was founded, and my uncle Philip Choy was one of the longtime leaders. He wasn’t a founder, but he was a longtime leader. And in 1969, which was supposed to be the celebration of the centennial anniversary of the completion of the transcontinental railroad, which was held in Utah and was celebrated by the U.S. government, there was a keynote speaker named John Volpe, he was the secretary of transportation. And he kept repeating, “it was American workers that built the railroad.” And he kept repeating “it was American workers that drove through tunnels of granite stone, through snow” and etcetera, etcetera. And the Chinese Historical Society protested, because in fact the Central Pacific Railroad was built mostly by Chinese immigrants who were not U.S. citizens. So this was 1969, May 1969, and at the same time I was ninth grade class president at a predominantly white student school. And I had to leave — to take a leave from school towards the end, before graduation, because my grandfather, who was the last living Chinese immigrant born, was dying. So when I read an article about what happened with the Chinese railroad workers being dismissed I was angry. I never ran for office again. You know prior to that I was often reminded that Stanford built the railroad. Well when I was growing up in 1963 we learned to sing songs in elementary school, songs such as “I’ve Been Working on the Railroad” and “Patty Builds the” — the Irish song. And then there was even the mythical John Henry, the mythical African-American hero was working faster. But there were no songs that valorized, no children’s songs that valorized Chinese immigrant workers who built the first transcontinental railroad. So then when I became a student at the Oberlin Conservatory of Music in Ohio in 1975, I took an African-American music course by professor Wendell Logan, who was department chair of African-American music. And I was introduced to the Afro-American music symphony by William Grant Still, which honored the African-American folk forms and sort of the storytelling of African- American life. It actually had the “I Got Rhythm” riff, which was something that William Grant Still created a melody when he was performing with I think Eubie Blake and the Shuffle-Along Orchestra in 1923. And Gershwin heard William Grant Still improvise it. Because you play the same music all the time. You know, Monk, you commented about how you had to play in a rock group, you know, you’re playing the same music and in a theatrical production you cannot improvise. So to kind of deal with the boredom at times you improvise before the production or the concert started. So then Gershwin, in 1930, he composed “I Got Rhythm” at the same time William Grant Still had the second movement “I Got Rhythm” theme in there. But in those days that was like, you know, the music was in the air.
Yeah. It was like Ellington listening to his guys warm up, and using pieces of their warm- up when writing a tune. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

Yeah. So how did I get to that. So anyway, I read a passage in Blues People by Leroi Jones, who is now known as Amiri Baraka. And in those days, I’m talking about the mid- 70’s, 1975, 1977, there were only two books on the reading list. There were probably a few more. But there was Blues People by Leroi Jones, and then The Music of Black Americans by Eileen Southern. So there weren’t that many. And I remember in the book by Amiri Baraka he talked about Africans brought over here as slaves, and they brought their songs with them. And then he mentioned that, but the feeling of doing labor in your own country is different than forced labor in another country. So that got me to thinking about well what about the Chinese who were brought over to the United States. Did they sing work songs and what did they sound like? So after the class was over I left the conservatory and I saw this sculpture of the underground railroad. Oberlin was a destination point for the underground railroad. And so there was a sculpture built. And I had this epiphany about someday composing a Chinese-American symphony. So 40 years later this dream came about when I was at an arts conference in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And I bumped into an Oberlin classmate who was a conductor, Michael Morgan. And we didn’t have a personal relationship. We had I think, we were really no different. He was a conductor in European music, I was studying piano performance. But I was interested in many different kinds of music. I was in a Javanese gamelan ensemble, a West African kora music ensemble, I studied composition, I performed in jazz ensembles, but I was a piano performance major, primarily eighteenth and nineteenth western European classical music. And I started late, at the age of 19. So I only had like two years under my belt. And that was considered taboo, to be exploring music outside of the eighteenth- nineteenth century western European hegemon. So it was a struggle and very, kind of stressful. But I saw it was very weary, the battle. I would describe it as an arts apartheid, or arts aparteid. I mean Stevie Wonder and those who were involved in South African liberation and struggles like in the 1980’s, we would pronounce it apartheid, not aparteid. But I mean I was active in that. That was one of the many struggles I was involved in as a political activist. But anyway, going back to my experience at Oberlin, as I said, yeah, 40 years later Michael Morgan, who was a conductor, he — somehow I introduced this idea to him and he thought well this would fit perfectly with the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra, which recently just received some funding for this California initiative to celebrate the history of California. And so the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra and the Oakland East Bay Symphony commissioned me to compose this work in 2006, and the work premiered, ironically, on the day that the Chinese set the record for laying down tracks in a single day, the number of miles, ten miles of track in a day. It beat the Irish, who were doing the Union Pacific Railroad. And that was April 28, 2007. Then in 2008, February 21, the Oakland East Bay Symphony premiered that work, and that was on the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-

day, I believe, that President Nixon made his visit to China. Before that, there wasn’t an open relationship between China and U.S. because of, you know, China being a communist government, the cold war period.

That’s a nice intersection of events. And it makes me think, I’m thinking about your composition process and the different musics that go into it. When I spoke — I did an interview with Toshiko Akiyoshi. And she had related when she was a kid, a child, she’s from Japan, but her father was working in China.
In Manchuria I believe.

And when she was studying piano she was learning Western — Bach. And I just thought what an interesting — a Japanese girl living in China, but she’s studying European music and it wasn’t until she went back to Japan around the end of World War II that she learned jazz. But she had — to make a long story short — she had to specifically seek out her own roots. So I’m wondering how and when did you get to explore — how did you explore traditional Chinese melodies which I assume that you wanted to include?

Well it took a lot of time. Because you see I also took ethnomusicology courses at Oberlin. And I was searching for those Chinese folk songs. But you have to understand that ethnomusicology, which was a marginalized field at that time, like they had a one- person faculty trying to do everything, and still today, you know, I mean for a long time you had everything except China, which is a large country, and maybe it was the political relationship between the U.S. and China, but if we even look specifically at the music of Asia, it was predominantly music of Japan, music of India, and gamelan. And you could see that with say Lou Harrison, you’ve had gamelan, although Henry Caio, who spent time in San Francisco, wrote some beautiful piano works, and then there’s Ruth Crawford Seeger who wrote, I think it was a vocal work using the text of H.T. Tsiang, who was a revolutionary artist at that time, and this was like the early 1930’s. I think it was 1931 or 1932. And Pearl Buck. She was ahead of her time. During the 1940’s she wrote this book, a collection, it was a couple named Chen, they wrote the music in western notation and Pearl Buck discussed it — or she wrote a preview about that. I think it was on John Day Publishing which was kind of progressive in those days. So there’s these — but other than that see it wasn’t until 1980 during dum chopain, the modernization, where of economic necessity that China began to open up, so you saw the emergency of Cantonese pop music from Hong Kong, Taiwan pop, and at the same time there was a large influx of books about Chinese music. So before, I think there was one book before 1980, maybe Music of China by Dr. Minu Tu. The other way I’ve found, or stumbled across, is Cantonese opera in the 1980’s when I lived in San Francisco. But if we look at the question why is the United States, whether you’re a lay person or academics, why are you more familiar with Japanese music than Chinese music? Well if you look at the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

process of assimilation, for example taiko, Japanese drums, came out of the Buddhist church and it was more part of mainstream America, and as a result we see there’s taiko groups and organizations throughout the United States and in Canada. But if we look at China, which is primarily an immigrant experience, the Cantonese opera is isolating it with the immigrant experience. It did not follow that same process until 1980. I mean today you have to look at two major Chinese music organizations — Music from China and New York, and Melodies of China and San Francisco.
Melodies of China?
Huh?
Did you say Melodies of China?

Melody. Melody of China. Which I’m not sure — I’ll make a reference to Paul Robeson. Because in the book Paul Robeson Speaks by Philip Foner, I think it’s on Beacon Hill Press back in the 1970’s, before Robeson passed. He was performing at Swarthmore College giving a lecture demonstration before that term was invented, because he’d always speak and frame the songs he was singing, which was the musics of the world, not just European tradition but also what he calls the Negro spirituals, I’d rename it the African-American spirituals, and he would say that in Africa, this is where you’d learn about rhythm. And he said in China, or maybe he said it was the Orient, it’s the melody. So in some ways I agree with what he was saying from the big picture perspective. I don’t think it’s that simple. But in a way he was coming from a place of respecting those traditions of the world. With European traditions he was talking about counterpoint. And that’s interesting about Bach, because in a lot of my study there’s, especially with train themes, a number of composers, they make a reference to Bach as being universal music.
As being what?

Well it’s sort of a universal connection maybe I should say. Not universal music. Actually it was more that Paul Robeson was nicknamed Mr. Pentatonic by Dizzy Gillespie. In one of my talks about Paul, tradition and transformation, — are you coming to the Tradition and Transformation presentation I’m giving today at 4:00?
Yes.

Yeah. I have an excerpt where Paul Robeson connects an African melody that predated Bach. An East African chorale forum he describes it, then syncs and eleventh century Czechoslovakian — it sounds like one melody. He seamlessly weaves it and this is predated Bach. And the reason why I said Bach is because when I studied different composers that have train themes there was a connection not only of the folk forms of those countries where those composers came from, but also there was a connection with the music of Bach. So for example, there was a Swiss composer named Arthur Honegger who lived in France and who was part of the Les Six, you know, the Darius Milhaud and © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

Erik Satie. And he wrote a piece in 1923 or 1924 called “Pacific 231.” And he recognized Bach as a major influence in the work. The music itself rates more of the technology — 231 is in reference to the axle design of the train. And to me that’s maybe related to the Italian futuristic movement, the art movement that had, you know, celebrated technology. And later on we see, in the 1930’s, the artist Diego Rivera, who painted those amazing Detroit industry murals celebrating not only technology but also the worker who made them, that technology, during the time of the Mexican repatriation act in the 1930’s. So then moving on, let’s see, that was 1923 to ’25 — in 1928 there was a composer from Shanghai named Li Jinhui who wrote a piece called “Express Train,” which sounded like the sound of a train but within a Chinese context. There’s a singer singing in Chinese and there’s a pentatonic melody specific — culturally specific Chinese way, which Li Jinhui by the way, created Chinese fusion music. He was probably the early example of Chinese fusion music. Because he and Buck Clayton in 1935 —
Buck Clayton, yeah.

He was in Shanghai in 1935 with his group, the Harlem Gentlemen, even though he was from Los Angeles. And that was because Duke Ellington was big during the advent of radio in the 1930’s, so in China they heard Duke Ellington, and so Buck Clayton took advantage of Ellington’s power, of his music, it was in New York, and called it the Harlem Gentlemen rather than Los Angeles. But, so they collaborated, that is Buck Clayton and Li Jinhui, and created this fusion of Chinese music and jazz. 1930 — well actually, a Bachianas — well yeah, a tribute to Bach, that Villa-Lobos, a Brazillian composer, who used folk forms but also he was honoring Bach, and his piece was the toccata, it was the “Little Train from Caipira,” which honored sort of the berry workers in Caipira which — I’m not pronouncing it correctly —
The what workers?
The berry workers. You know, the farm workers, I’m sorry.
Oh, the berry.

The farm workers, yeah. That’s actually a bit less specific, but, yeah, the farm workers. Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, maybe it was more of Billy Strayhorn, you know it’s so hard to kind of separate one from the other, but the “Daybreak Express,” 1932 I think. And I think it was 1958, “Track 360,” that’s an amazing work, one minute. I think it’s one minute or two minutes long. And then, well, Steve Reich’s “Different Trains” in 1988, for string quartet and recordings. So I immersed myself in all this music, and it’s like Charlie Parker said, you practice, or you study, and then you forget everything. And so I felt that I wanted to honor composers, you know I didn’t want to judge what they did, I wanted to try to take whatever I could learn from what they did and then kind of see what would happen. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-

You had mentioned in the interview from ten years ago, it’s a bit of a paraphrase here, but you said that the Chinese are not ready for what I’m offering. And I wasn’t quite sure if you were talking about Chinese-Americans or that you were trying to see if you could get your music played in China. Do you remember? And is it still the case?
Well I’m pretty clear on that, it was people in China.
Oh, okay.

Because well we see Min Xiao-Fen is performing with me on pipa. And when Chinese come over here there’s that social interaction, the musical interaction, and then they become sort of the modern Chinese-born American. Whereas, and you could see, well I’ll give you an example of two great leaders: Mao Tse Tung, okay? So there’s a story about one of the Chinese saxophonists who was older than me by about twenty years, who performed for Mao. And Chou En-lai, who studied in the west, studied in Paris, was friends with W.E.B. Debois, and was jazz was played he was dancing. And Mao was pretty stiff. So when Chinese are exposed to — and there’s young Chinese who study overseas and they return to say Beijing — in fact I was interviewed in a publication called “That’s Beijing,” which is an English publication, and that’s for the intellectual middle-class, upper-class Chinese who are residing in a specific group — there are these, to me, the potential of these young modern Chinese-born citizens. But then there’s those who are, say if your whole world is within China, and that depends whether you’re in the city or the country, I mean China is a large country. So because China has so many people, and it’s a large country, you know, you know the communist party had to have a certain amount of control, out of practical purposes. You know, the highly centralized form of democratic centralism, if you put it in Marxist terms, which is different than say the Soviet Union. Because China has a long history, 256 years during the Ching dynasty and years of feudalism, and so it’s a remarkable transformation in the twentieth century. But of course you know there’s other —

Well last week, timely, there was a couple of Chinese students. I’m not even sure they were teaching assistants, they did an hour program on Chinese popular music. One did something she called Chinese rock & roll. And the other one did, and I wish I had written the word down, there was a term that apparently there’s a popular style that combines almost hip hop, that kind of thing, using traditional Chinese instruments. It was very interesting. And it’s amazing how pervasive Western pop music is now around the world. And I wonder if you’ve been to China and heard what they’re doing now as far as young people’s music?

Well I think perhaps what you’re suggesting is that there is maybe another transformation with the younger generation? I performed with Cui Jian who is the rock icon of China — China’s first rock icon I should say. As a result I had nothing but my name. He expressed © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

the collective feelings of his generation, you know Tiananmen Square was like 1989. And next year will be the 25th anniversary. But Cui Jian expressed the sentiments of those young students at that time, who felt alienated from the cultural revolution. And so the 1980’s was the emergence of rock, but there wasn’t, you know rock represented rebellion, I guess, of the government. And so it was an expression of that but not necessarily — there was a motivation to think of yourself as an artist and trying to develop something with that music, or develop something that’s distinctively either Chinese or distinctively about that individual, or both. You know I actually don’t separate that. So I guess the other part, the earlier question you mentioned about whether the Chinese embrace what I’m offering is that, like I say there’s sort of a compartmentalization to — and sort of the intellectual process too. So that’s why I’m saying that for those who have studied overseas they can develop a broader perspective. And actually to me, you could go back to the students at the May 4, 1990, you know, that movement. And what was very important — you know that was that big ah out of Bejing University — that the students felt it was important to preserve folk songs. And see to me the folk songs were like songs of survival, in much the same way as the African- American spirituals. So the songs of survival have a very soulful feeling. And that’s why I’m drawn to it. I’m just — I mean I’ve accepted the fact that we’re okay — just put something Chinese there, that’s what it is. But the concert we’re going to give for example, this Friday, with Dr. Michael Woods, we, at a rehearsal, talked about the “Flower Drum Song,” which originated in the Ming dynasty when China was very strong and didn’t really need foreign contact. They felt very confident. And there’s a song called the “Flower Drum Song” which is performed by a husband and a wife during times of poverty. They were like street musicians. And the “Flower Drum Song” was a playful exchange of insults because if you do something funny people give you money. And I said it was like the Chinese dozens. And the dozens is also a playful exchange of insults in African-American tradition. So Doc Woods said, your mamma’s so fat, you know, she could not, you know, etcetera, etcetera. Well you’re from my generation, you know, like from “The Jeffersons,” that television show in the 1970’s, when George Jefferson would perform that ritual of the dozens. So then I did my shameless English translation of the “Flower Drum Song,” the wife would say to the husband well you’re no good ‘cause you’re not making any money, you’re not in the magistrate, you’re not in government — well there wasn’t a government — but you’re not making any money. The husband would go back to the wife and say well you’re no good ‘cause you’re ugly because you have big feet — because during the Ming dynasty there was the practice of the unbound feet which would keep women in their place and not to leave the village. So that was kind of a great sharing of experience, you know, with Doc Woods and the students too. And © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-

then I had gone through, to me, the change of tradition, the tradition of transformation in China. That “Flower Drum Song” became an important cultural device for the Chinese communist party to recruit illiterate peasants in the countryside. You’d have a performance of the “Flower Drum Song” that was something familiar to peasants to draw them in, and then later on, in 1945, [s/l] Yuan Nin, who was an actress from Shanghai and also a member of the communist party, performed it in, I think it was March of 1945 towards the end of Roosevelt’s days. I mean Roosevelt, President Roosevelt died I think in April of 1945. She performed the “Flower Drum Song.” And then we see that there was a novel in 195 — what was it, 7? — by C.Y. Lee, that was part of another lost generation, which was made into a Broadway musical by Rodgers & Hammerstein, and that was significant because it made a film in 1961 which was kind of loosely based on, or loosely inspired by Forbidden City, one of the early, but not the first, early Chinatown nightclubs in San Francisco. And so I mean why is that significant? Because there was no films that featured Asian-American actors in a very human way until 1992, I think it was Wayne Wang, “Joy Luck Club.” So that was significant about Rodgers & Hammerstein. If Hammerstein had lived, because he died I think around the release of the film in 1961, had he lived longer, who knows what could have happened. I know I’m getting — are you going to edit this?
Oh we might.
Oh okay. Because that’s why I’m talking. Just try to tell me what you want me — to guide me. See I’m older now so now I’ve got the longer stories.

Well ten years ago, once again, I asked you what you thought of the state of the country. That’s an easy question, isn’t it? And you said, your answer was fairly spiritual I thought. And you quoted Max Roach who we talked about earlier today, who said I can’t save the world. But then you talked about the “River of Life.” And so I feel like asking the question again, what do you — let’s talk about the state of the country first, on this particular day when we have this gridlock and so forth. Do you have any particular thoughts about the state of our country?
Well it’s, yes, I mean my presentations kind of represent that. So you were present at the One Day American/One Day Alien, persons of color who changed the national anthem —
Yes.

I mean we have a divided country. And I’ll give you an example. I was a visiting professor at University of Michigan last November during the election. And I was staying in a hotel and there was one elderly white woman who was a native of Ann Arbor, Michigan, but I think somewhat far away from the university it seems, or she really didn’t have a connection. And she was disabled, and we had a friendly interaction, and I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

was trying to help her with the chair and she said it was nice. And she was complaining about where she lived, that she was on the second floor. And I said well can’t you change with the person on the bottom floor so you don’t have to go up the steps. The next day after Barack Obama was elected president she just went into a tirade. “I didn’t vote for communism, I didn’t vote for socialism, I’m going to leave the country.” And you know I supported Barack Obama, but if Mitt Romney had been elected I wouldn’t have been so emotional about it. I did not vote for both George Bushes or Ronald Reagan, but that — and it reminded me of my presentation, how one side of the country just overly reacts as being anti-American.
And there was talk about, when Obama went into office, would this herald the start of the post-racial society. And it has not looked like it.

Well, so my role, and I’ll go back, I was elected ninth grade president. Because I think people, they like me, either my personality, I mean I had relationships with the jocks, who were generally more conservative, I had relationships with more of the alternative artists, intellectual hippy types. And if I perform the “Star Spangled Banner” National Anthem, depending on the context, I can perform it in the tradition of John Phillip Sousa on the piano, or I can first perform it in the traditional way and then go into another version and then come back to it. So I can take music and bring people — it helps resolve the differences. So it’s kind of like hey, we all share the same food, we can all go out to different restaurants, but we all don’t have to like certain foods. And so that’s the same thing. Different versions of the National Anthem. And I also have friends who, you know, they react to — how can I describe it — I want to try to be respectful — say of the Tea Party republicans. To me there is — you know you don’t want to be emotionally reactive to that either. Because that also doesn’t really — I guess it’s kind of crisis management or anger management. And actually in some ways I thought Barack Obama was trying to unite the country. And I’ll give you an example. I like the idea of having Beyonce collaborate with the Marine Band. I liked the idea. However, Barack Obama is not an artist or involved in cultural production. So if you want to have that collaboration, and you want to quote unquote arts to succeed, you have to have it inside. Or you have to have both of them be prerecorded, and can kind of accept that. And I think, as I said before, the American Bandstand legacy, we forget about that. And we also forget that, hey, what is the big deal about that, because I mean MTV — the emphasis is on the visual aspect. I mean Michael Jackson or anybody else cannot dance and sing at the same time. That’s too – when we hear singers, whether it’s opera — their instrument is the voice. And it’s very difficult to do that.
You mean dancing and singing. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

I mean that’s like me dancing while I’m playing the piano. I mean I guess Jerry Lee Lewis, I don’t know if you call it dancing but there’s a movement. But I don’t see very many people doing that. And I suppose you could.

I think it’s curious, those controversial performances, the “Star Spangled Banner” and these sports teams or whatever, they hire these people and then they’re so surprised and sometimes angry when the person sings like they do. Like you were expecting Marvin Gaye to sing the national anthem like an opera singer or like someone with great respect. And he sings it like he wants to and everybody gets bent out of shape. And it’s just curious that, well why are you hiring these people then, if you don’t want them to sing like they do.

Yeah. And I mean that was Marvin Gaye who won the coveted Grammy award for “Sexual Healing.” And then the ironic part is that the melody of the “Star Spangled Banner” by John Stafford Smith was an 18th century British sex and drinking song, so actually and ironically Marvin Gaye was actually respecting the tradition of where it came from, which is actually Brit — I mean “America the Beautiful,” actually that was by two composers — the melody was from Samuel Augustus Ward, and then Katharine Lee Bates. And that’s powerful, because it was a woman composer, an American woman composer. And so there was talk about changing the national anthem from the “Star Spangled Banner” to “America the Beautiful.” That was actually 1989 by Senator Andrew Jacobs, who was a democrat from Indiana, and he was a disabled Marine veteran. So what was great about that — not whether he was a democrat or republican — is that he said well we should not abandon the “Star Spangled Banner,” it should be for specific, like military — you know because the military is about sort of you can’t — it’s no nonsense, see that’s the whole culture. You know you have to — any kind of deviation and that’s uncalled for. And it has to be, because you’re at war your whole life. So I understand that. And that’s why I would play it, if I perform it, I would respect that. Because these are people that are fighting for your country. But then if you also want to say think out of the box, and even if you think of the creative process, which was not a collaboration between John Stafford Smith and Francis Scott Key — Francis Scott Key took something and he made something new out of it, right? Because the words was not about Anacreon, it was not about the god of love and pleasure, of wine and women, it was about being captive on the ship and seeing your country being bombed, and then the flag is there. And he’s an amateur lawyer, or amateur poet and he’s a lawyer. But he was inspired to write words to it. So the story about that — and that was something that you could argue was not only inspiring but sort of, you know, he was changing the tradition of the song. So, you know, I think we need to look deeply into the history and deeply — instead of this reaction. So that’s why I don’t think of it as hey, these are the republicans © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-

that are over there, these are the democrats that are over there, these are the Marines. I think in some ways Barack Obama tried to bring the country together. I mean he had Aretha Franklin sing “My Country ‘Tis of Thee,” which is actually only like six pitches in range, vocal range, an easy song to sing. And this time he had what, like Kelly Clarkson, you know? So I mean he had a multi-cultural — he had classical music and art — Aaron Copland. He had “Simple Gifts” the time before. So he’s — I mean that’s what impressed me was his inauguration. The artists that need to be included, not just the celebrities, but we’re all together. And I also, yeah, I mean Beyonce and Jay-Z, I know that they were criticized by Harry Belafonte who is somebody that I greatly respect. But they cannot be, you know, they’re black artists but they have a role that they can contribute. I think as I grow older I’m trying to not expect the younger generation to follow what I’ve done or even my predecessors. It’s just like — well my daughter for example, is 18 years old. She has to find her journey. And hopefully the value of integrity and being honest and doing what’s real is most important.

Have you noticed, we also had talked a little bit about people’s attention span. And this was ten years ago. And now things have — the demands on our attention, multi-tasking etcetera, have greatly increased. Does that affect your audience do you think? Are they affected by that?

Well you’re interviewing me. I can’t lay out this long history. Because history is not sexy. And we had spoke about Malcolm Gladwell’s A Tipping Point. There has to be a stickiness. And you have to sort of go for it, and then we are also living in a highly competitive economic society and people don’t have the time, they’re overscheduled and you really have to like — it’s almost like being in New York in the zoo. You’ve got to — no matter if you lay out your best shot, it may not be embraced, you may not get that opportunity, etcetera, etcetera. So having this opportunity to be interviewed I can speak more freely and at length, but yes, if I’m in a live performance there’s just a lot of different aspects that I have to reconsider. So I don’t perform as much but it seems like in some ways I feel a loyalty to the artists that have developed my music. But then I understand in a certain sense why Art Blakey had — well from my perspective, not from Art Blakey’s — when he started to hire younger musicians. I mean part of it is transmission — trying to nurture the younger generation. But partly it is also bringing younger audiences to the concerts. So I think now I have to — I’ll have to consider that but what’s difficult is why would young artists want to hang socially with an old guy like me? And then I guess I shouldn’t really criticize or put myself down because hey, for me, being with — I mean I was mentored by Max Roach. He was the age of my father. Max Roach was like a father figure. I’m not sure if that — well maybe I don’t think highly enough of myself, but I’m not sure — well yeah, maybe I could play that role. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-
What did Max Roach have that was unique? What was unique about Max Roach?

He was very noble. I remember when we performed Duke Ellington’s “Come Sunday” I could see the humble and humility. And I mean he was a real warrior and you know, some of the works I pay tribute some of the great artists, like Paul Robeson and Mei Manfang. You know I’m trying to respect those artists who’ve become forgotten. Or like I would say one day American — or one day great American artists and one day alien, with a persecution, and the unofficial ban on Paul Robeson’s life during the McCarthy period of the 1950’s, but he’s one of the greatest American artists. And so I pay tribute to him. When Max Roach, when I saw him perform with Sid Catlett on the hi-hat, see there’s that stickiness, that personality. What he does on the hi-hat, a solo piece, and then it brings your attention to who was Sid Catlett? I mean I’m finding — there may be students here that don’t know who Max Roach is. So now I’ve been thinking about, well God, there’s so many legacies I feel — I don’t know if I have to say protect, or if I have to try to preserve. And then there’s my own legacy. Because it’s been — but then now I have to accept that I have no control over that. Now Max, when I was working with him, he rejected the term jazz. In fact, one of the working titles of his book that he working on Max was “Jazz is a Four Letter Word.” Because his reference is to fornication. You know it came out of the New Orleans bordellos. Louis Armstrong hated New Orleans, although he said that Louis Armstrong was the most political person because he saw Louis Armstrong’s face, a smiling face, and then he saw the weariness and sorrow in a hotel room. So he saw the power and sorrow of Louis Armstrong. You know Max Roach, I mean he was a person of integrity. When we recorded the Beijing Trio he — well for me, I thought okay let’s call it the Max Roach Jon Jang Duo. You know, have his name first, this way we could attract more listeners, sell more CD’s. But he really believed in the collective. You know this music is about democracy. And he wanted to call it the Beijing Trio. So like his group M’Boom — it’s not the Max Roach — and I think on an earlier recording he wanted to focus on, was it “Hasaan”? Incredible pianist recording, I think it was in 1965 on Atlantic. But he had an original voice. And that’s one of the things that Max Roach really embraced about my — not really the way I perform on piano, but my thinking. So actually when I approached him about “SenseUs: The Rainbow Anthems,” and that was to reconceptualize the Star Spangled anthem — the national anthem — why does the national anthem have to be a song? Why can’t it be a poem? Why can’t the national anthem — why is it only one national anthem? Why can’t there be more anthems that speak to the majority of people in this country? And why is the “Star Spangled Banner,” which is a celebration of war, why is it that for most people, who can only sing an octave, eight pitches, why do we sing the national anthem which has twelve pitches? And if most of us cannot sing the national anthem, then essentially the national anthem is © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

undemocratic. So anyway there’s so much that I’ve learned from Max Roach, and it helped validate the direction of where I’m going and who I am. So it’s taken me years to reflect. And also I had to realize, or learn to realize, because of lot of us, like our heroes when we’re young, that I had a friendship but also a friendship with someone who — you know when you think about heroes there’s this immortality and they’re perfect. But we all have problems. And one of them was deteriorating health. But what inspired me was that hey, he was in his 70’s. And the concert we did in Milano, Italy was incredible, in 2001. And then in 2002 in Los Angeles, I mean I couldn’t believe — he was like I think Max Roach described it he says it’s like I never stopped learning to ride the bicycle. It was like he was in his 20’s or 30’s or 40’s, still he was the great Max Roach. And my goals, now that I’m approaching 60 years of age, I’m inspired by Max Roach to pursue, pursue, pursue. I’m inspired by Duke Ellington, who was composing music on his deathbed. I’m inspired by Giuseppe Verdi, who wrote full staff, an opera, a comic opera, when he was 80 years old, or Akira Kurosawa, who was making his last film in his 80’s, or Pablo Casals, who I think he recorded some Bach suites in his 90’s and he said he was practicing and he finally learned how to play them right, or something outrageous like that. And you know, it brings to me Pablo Picasso. The English translation of what he said, he said it takes a long time to become young. And what he was talking about is everyone knows well who was the first president of the United States, two and two is equal to four, or from some Asians who are really great in math, the quadratic formula, which you’ve got to fit in a circle, what’s the opposite of B plus or minus — well why is it either/or you know? The opposite of B, plus or minus the square root of B square minus 4AC over 2A. You know? But Pablo Picasso was talking about discovering what’s unique about you in your planet. There’s only one Jon Jang. So it’s about the music of Jon Jang. The changing music of Jon Jang. There’s the music of Max Roach. There’s the music of Monk Rowe. You know, that’s when I say Thelonious Monk — always? No. Always Rowe. Monk? Always Rowe? No?

I wanted to ask you about your composition and the topics and the song titles. Most of your work looks to be allegorical or story driven, historical driven. Have you ever — I’m trying to figure out how to ask this — have you ever had music that comes to you that doesn’t have a specific intent?

Well yeah. The example is “I Feel the Thunder in My Heart” on Tiananmen. Because I was — I think I was practicing on a broken down upright piano in San Francisco Chinatown, and suddenly the thunder struck. And I could feel it through my body. And then I could relate that experience with the making of “Take My Hand Precious Lord” by Thomas A. Dorsey, who composed that — you know it’s one of the hymns of African- American people. And the story is that after his wife and child died during childbirth, he © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

wanted to give up music, just wanted to play the blues, I think give up music in the church. And then he saw this image of the rock, I think above him, and there was like water, or tears, pouring down on the keys of the piano. And then he created the song. So I mean it wasn’t the same kind of experience, and of course in my case I wrote it was nothing like — nowhere close to the power of what he wrote. But to me that is like the music doesn’t come to me, it comes through me. And sometimes the process is like I’m in the shower and singing, and I’m allowing the water to beat meaninglessly against my body. And that’s kind of what I loved about Bruce Lee, and oh yes, going back to the piece that you aired on the radio called “Falling Stream.” The reason why we came to that title was Max Roach and I talked about “King Joe” and Count Basie, which was the way to honor Joe Louis. So I talked to him about Bruce Lee. And how I got into music was at the same time, after Keystone Korner, was Rahsaan Roland Kirk, a performance at Keystone Korner in June 1973, dropped out of U.C. Berkeley and started piano on the day that John Coltrane died, the anniversary of the day that John Coltrane died, the sixth anniversary. It was July 17, 1973, I had my first piano lesson. And then Bruce Lee died in July, 1973. And then Enter the Dragon came out. And if you look at — there’s a scene where Bruce Lee’s mentoring this young Chinese kid and he says emotional content, not anger. And that was what John Coltrane was about. The jazz critics started attacking John Coltrane, anti-jazz, just like anti-American. You know? And his music is angry and it was really about emotional content. And so that’s how I drew the parallels between John Coltrane and Bruce Lee. And Bruce Lee, it’s not all about this martial — I’ll kick your ass. It’s about expression of his humanity. And in some ways, just movement. And if you listen to recordings with Max Roach, that’s what — the movement is what he does on percussion from a lower register sounding of his tom-toms, to the cymbals, the higher register. And what I do in the upper register and lower register, and there’s this kind of conversation of movement. And I’m trying to remember “King Joe” — I don’t think it was about that. And then it was Paul Robeson singing it. You know, and Count Basie, his music was blues and Paul Robeson was like more of a classical singer. Anyway, so I’m sorry, I tend to digress and move into something else, but —

Well titles can be interesting because they certainly can affect a listener’s experience before they hear anything. You know, if you see this title, you had a title about capital punishment I think. So if you see that, sometimes I relate it to looking at an abstract work of art, that I would rather not see the title first. I’d rather look at it without that thing in my head. Because I might be looking, the title says this, okay where is it in the work? Anyway I’ve always been sort of fascinated with titles because, you know the classical composers, they have those sort of generic things that they could use. Like “Air on a G © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-
String.” Well does that mean that that music doesn’t have a meaning besides the fact that it’s beautiful music?

Well I understand what you’re — I understand your question, because you’re inferring about whether music has programmatic aspects to it. Or at least that’s one part of it. That’s not necessarily the whole part. But I would say that sometimes these titles, they come through me at the particular time. So “River of Life” is actually from Revelation and after 9/11 the pastor, a woman pastor, offered the Scripture. And it was very — the Bible has very poetic scriptures. And one of the last lines is that leaves are for the healing of the nation. So the “River of Life” and as well as the “Tree of Life” that was something that I had embraced at that particular time, and that’s why I came up with the title. Actually one of the persons that was involved in the recording — who I won’t mention because he wasn’t really a producer — wanted to call it “capital punishment.” But it was too literate. That’s not how I felt. I mean we did make a statement about — to portraits of capital punishment. And then for Beijing Trio Max Roach asked me to — or he actually assigned me to get the titles because he liked the “Two Flowers on a Stem.” So that’s why you have “Sweet Whisper of a Flower,” that’s sort of from an English translation of a Cantonese poem — a Cantonese love poem. Cantonese is the southern language of China, which is where my ancestors are from. So yeah, it’s different. But usually it’s what’s happened — well no I can’t say, I can’t really give you a generalization. Sometimes there’s something that’s happened with me in the present, and sometimes it is this historical recovery is part of the creative process. But one of the other things you’re suggesting is that — well one other part of your question is why can’t you just name it piece 110, 11, well like Anthony Braxton. Or say Beethoven Sonata, Opus 26 in A flat major. You know I mean, well okay I can partially answer that question too off of one story. The making of “Portrait of Sun Yat-sen,” which will be performed this Friday — I was commissioned by the Chinese Cultural Foundation in San Francisco to celebrate the centennial anniversary of the Xinhai, or the Chinese Revolution of 1911. And this revolution was that the Chinese Revolution defeated the Manchus, the Ching Dynasty, after 256 years of rule. And so I wanted to honor Dr. Sun Yat-sen, who was the revolution leader, the father of modern China. And I was inspired by the model of “Lincoln Portrait” by Aaron Copland, who was commissioned by Kostelanetz. There was — shortly — in response to the bombing of Pearl Harbor in 1941. So Aaron Copland was very active in the popular front. He was considered a gay communist, with a small c. He didn’t belong to the communist part of the United States, you know this is according to Fanfare for the Common Man, Aaron Copland during the Depression Years. But the popular front was this popular left wing social phenomenon that — let’s see — was this coalition of okay the communist part of the U.S.A., independent communists, © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-

progressives, social democrats, liberals, Roosevelt-new dealers — it was a kind of a united front or a coalition. And of course you know about, because of that movement, you know Roosevelt created the Works Progress Administration, which provided work for artists, you know, and sometimes labor union contexts. And Aaron Copland wanted to — one of his musical goals was that we need to change the music so that it would become more accessible to the public. Because the public was alienated by sort of the you know, the Schoenberg’s utilization. And so that was one reason why, you know, I write these works that have programmatic titles. The other reason is that we forget about history, and these important great artists such as Paul Robeson, or, you know, a great leader of modern China, Sun Yat-sen. And also, the relationship of Sun Yat-sen was inspired by Lincoln. They both wanted to unify their countries by building the railroad. Lincoln through the Railroad Act of 1862. He never saw it realized. It was completed by Chinese immigrants in 1869. He could envision it. Because he died before that. Or Sun Yat-sen, he was ahead of his time. I guess China was not unified. It was dominated by foreign imperialists, you know, the Ching dynasty — a large country with bandits and so forth — it was undeveloped. So that’s partly why at this point in my life, you know, where legacy is very important —
That leads me to —
And also I want to connect it with Max Roach’s honoring of Sid Catlett.

Okay. Well our tape is going to run out soon. I wanted to say, or ask, if we did Part III interview at some point in a few years, is there something that you would like to be able to say that I accomplished this, between now and a few years from now. Do you have some specific goal you’re working on right now?

Well I — what I think is we should — I’m really glad that you’re going to be able to make the “Traditions Transformation” presentation. Because out of this interview, you know I could talk story, music story, for a long time. So I think it’s more like I need to show you more of what I’m doing and then that’s going to come up with some other questions. Now whether I directly address them or maybe I take an improvisation in another direction — and I am improvising. I mean of course it’s all a lot of content information that I accumulated over the years, and they go in like different directions. And they’re always going to go in different directions. So I can’t really answer that. But I will tell you that I feel very satisfied because I generally don’t get a chance to do these kind of interviews where you’d allow me to talk. Because a lot of times I’m already categorized. Or if someone asked me about, you didn’t even use the term “Asian- American jazz” — which I don’t — you know my colleagues and friends Anthony Brown and Mark Izu, that’s very important to them. And it’s an important — I don’t censor that part of it, but it’s not that important for me. I mean I’ve got so many things to © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -17-

talk about, but it doesn’t — I’m not sure it really expresses who I am. So and we can’t go into the whole — I mean I already spent too much time on my childhood, about the railroad. But yet, actually, let me put it another way. If you’re interested, on YouTube I recently was awarded the History Maker award by the Chinese Historical Society of America, last month. That was September 21st. And they did a three minute YouTube, or a three or four minute YouTube. And I open up where I saw well I’m just like my father, who I didn’t know, he died when I was two years old. And I said during the 1930’s, my father, who was five-foot two, would dance with a six-foot two blonde, you know, which was taboo. And then, so he would — I think I made a statement that says most Chinese Americans I know, of my generation, are afraid to take chances. So for me, it’s like you do it. It’s like Bruce Lee, you don’t have time to think. Actually Bruce Lee said thinking without thinking. Which I’m wondering, Malcolm Gladwell wrote the book Blink. I don’t know if you’re familiar with that. That’s the second book after Tipping Point. It’s called thinking without thinking. But he does not identify with Bruce Lee at all in that book. But that’s who I am is the thinking without thinking. Oh and also, okay, as artists, we embrace paradox. So oh, that’s what it is about this country. You know it’s black and white. People want the black and white answers. Just like the national anthem. Artists, we embrace paradox. And I’ll say one more thing is that James Baldwin wrote a powerful response to James Lincoln Collier’s The Making of Jazz which was published in 1979, James Lincoln Collier the prominent writer who graduated from Hamilton College in 1952. And James Lincoln Collier wrote this article in 1979, it was called “The Cross of Redemption, of Sorrow Songs.” And it got republished recently. That’s the title of the book. It’s only seven pages long. But he will say you can’t study history from a distance. Then he comes back and contradicts himself and says you can study history from a safe distance. So that’s a perfect — it’s a powerful article. And when we’re finished recording I’d like to get your perspective and reflections about The Making of Jazz both from the book and your interview with James Lincoln Collier.

Well this has been fascinating, once again. And I wish you the best of luck with your concert on Friday, and as a pianist and composer and thinker — and I think you called yourself a “cultural entrepreneur?”
Yeah, Steve Yao did. Professor Steve Yao.
Yes, that’s right.
I said “social entrepreneur.” Yeah that is, well one way to define it that is one who engages in a process that solves social problems with innovative solutions.
Nice. All right.
And we do it through music and though I guess being a public intellectual — or multiple ways. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -18-
Right. Well thanks for your time again.
Well thank you, Monk. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -19-

segments.title: Copyright statement and interview introduction
segments.summary: Boilerplate, biographical note and setting of the 2013 Part II interview at Hamilton College.

segments.title: Becoming the first American-born Chinese composer of a symphony
segments.summary: Jang says he composed 'The Chinese-American Symphony' honoring Chinese railroad workers; the idea germinated in his Palo Alto childhood.

segments.title: Railroad history, the 1969 protest, and William Grant Still at Oberlin
segments.summary: Stanford and the railroad, the 1969 centennial protest by the Chinese Historical Society, missing songs for Chinese workers, and learning of Still's Afro-American Symphony at Oberlin in 1975.

segments.title: Oberlin epiphany and the 2006 symphony commission
segments.summary: Reading Blues People sparked the idea of a Chinese-American symphony; forty years later Michael Morgan helped get it commissioned and premiered in 2007 and 2008.

segments.title: Seeking traditional Chinese melodies and the neglect of Chinese music
segments.summary: Prompted by Rowe's Toshiko Akiyoshi story, Jang explains the lack of Chinese music in ethnomusicology and why Japanese music assimilated more easily.

segments.title: Paul Robeson, melody, and Bach as a universal connection
segments.summary: Jang discusses Robeson's remarks about rhythm and melody, his nickname Mr. Pentatonic, and Bach as a link among composers of train themes.

segments.title: Train-themed compositions from Honegger to Steve Reich
segments.summary: A survey of train pieces: Pacific 231, Li Jinhui's Express Train and Buck Clayton in Shanghai, Villa-Lobos, Ellington/Strayhorn, Reich; Jang's approach to absorbing them.

segments.title: Are the Chinese ready for his music? China versus Chinese-Americans
segments.summary: Jang clarifies his earlier remark referred to people in China, contrasting Chinese-born artists abroad with those whose world is within China.

segments.title: Cui Jian, Chinese rock, folk songs, and the Flower Drum Song
segments.summary: Rowe asks about young Chinese music; Jang recalls performing with rock icon Cui Jian, Tiananmen, and the preservation of folk songs.

segments.title: Flower Drum Song in the Communist Party and on Broadway
segments.summary: Jang compares the Flower Drum Song to the dozens, traces its use by the Communist Party and its Rodgers and Hammerstein adaptation, and worries about rambling.

segments.chapter: State of the country and the anthem
segments.title: State of the country and a divided America
segments.summary: Asked about the nation today, Jang tells of a hotel encounter in Ann Arbor after Obama's reelection; Rowe raises the post-racial hope.

segments.chapter: State of the country and the anthem
segments.title: Music as a way to bridge differences, Obama and Beyonce with the Marine Band
segments.summary: Jang describes performing the national anthem in different versions, being class president, and views on Obama's use of the arts.

segments.chapter: State of the country and the anthem
segments.title: National anthem controversies, Marvin Gaye and the origins of the Star Spangled Banner
segments.summary: Rowe notes controversial anthem performances; Jang covers the tune's origins, America the Beautiful, and Francis Scott Key as creative transformer.

segments.title: Attention span, history not being sexy, and mentoring younger musicians
segments.summary: Jang talks about audiences' short attention, the stickiness of stories, Art Blakey hiring younger players, and being mentored by Max Roach.

segments.title: Max Roach's nobility, rejection of 'jazz', and the Beijing Trio
segments.summary: Jang portrays Max Roach as noble and collective-minded, covering Sid Catlett, the Beijing Trio name and the SenseUs anthem project.

segments.title: Lessons from Max Roach and inspiration from artists who kept creating
segments.summary: Jang reflects on Roach's final years, concerts in 2001-02, and elders who created into old age, and Picasso's remark about becoming young.

segments.title: Music that comes through him: Thunder in My Heart, Dorsey, Bruce Lee
segments.summary: Asked about music without specific intent, Jang describes 'I Feel the Thunder in My Heart' and compares it to Dorsey's Precious Lord.

segments.title: Song titles, River of Life, Beijing Trio, and Sun Yat-sen portrait
segments.summary: Rowe muses about titles; Jang explains the origins of River of Life, Capital Punishment, and Beijing Trio titles.

segments.title: Copland, the Popular Front, and why Jang writes programmatic works
segments.summary: Jang describes his commission for the 1911 revolution centennial, Copland's Lincoln Portrait, the Popular Front and accessible music.

segments.title: Closing questions about future goals and Asian-American jazz labels
segments.summary: Rowe asks about future goals; Jang says he feels satisfied to talk at length and that the Asian-American jazz label is not central for him.

segments.title: History Maker award, thinking without thinking, and Baldwin on The Making of Jazz
segments.summary: Jang cites a YouTube tribute, Bruce Lee and Gladwell's Blink, embracing paradox, and James Baldwin's response to James Lincoln Collier.

segments.title: Social entrepreneur and goodbyes
segments.summary: They discuss the label 'cultural' or 'social entrepreneur' and thank each other to end the interview.
